- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then underestimates later days.
- Forecasts tend to overshoot after sharp price spikes (e.g., 80+), then sharply correct downward — model fails to capture this “rebound” or “mean reversion” effect.
- Model exhibits persistent bias toward higher prices in the first 10–15 days of the forecast window, especially when history shows recent upward momentum.
- When true prices drop sharply (e.g., from 80 to 60+), model fails to adjust downward quickly — often underestimates the magnitude of the drop.
- Model tends to ignore recent downward trends in the history window, especially if they are recent (last 5–7 days), leading to overconfident upward forecasts.
- Forecasts are often too smooth — fail to capture volatility spikes or sudden reversals in the last 5–10 days of history.
- Model underestimates the impact of “low-price” periods in the history window — especially when recent prices are below 70, model still forecasts higher than true.
- Model overreacts to short-term volatility — forecasts spike after minor price movements, then fail to correct.
- Model tends to “anchor” on the most recent high price, even if it’s not the true trend — leading to overestimation of future prices.
- Model underestimates the effect of “seasonal” or “calendar-driven” price drops (e.g., end-of-month, holiday periods) — often fails to adjust for known patterns.
